titles: Research into vector control for malaria and other mosquito-borne diseases.
descriptions: Research into vector control for malaria and other mosquito-borne diseases.
Research on the cost-effective use of malaria vector control interventions; and future threats from mosquito-borne diseases

To address the most pressing challenges in vector control for malaria and other mosquito-borne diseases.The world’s biggest vector control challenges are malaria in tropical Africa and Aedes-borne viruses which also pose the most dangerous future threats. This RPC will focus on the key constraints limiting the cost-effectiveness of interventions. In Africa, the key threat is the growing challenge of insecticide resistance in malaria mosquitoes. Although new tools have been developed to help overcome this threat, there is less evidence on which interventions to prioritise according to the resistance in the target area. In the case of Aedes mosquitoes, the problem is even deeper - the evidence-base for intervention efficacy is remarkably weak. The RPC will address these issues through methodological innovation in trial design for randomised trials. Additionally the research will consider resilience,and the capacity of vector control systems to respond to future threats and opportunities.

This programme is designed to address the multifaceted challenges faced by children in camps and communities in East Syria, particularly those deprived of liberty, children impacted by conflict, and internally displaced children. titles: Business Case Appraisal & Design Budget
descriptions: This programme will support a substantial reduction in plastic waste generation through impact across five key areas (tbc during programme design); a) Research & Evidence, b) Design & Innovation, c) Catalytic Funding, d) Enabling environments, e) Building Capacity.  It will contribute to results including a reduction in the amount of plastic waste entering the oceans and a decrease in negative environmental impacts associated with poor plastic waste management, notably flood risk from the blockage of drainage systems and ambient air pollution due to burning of waste. titles: GGGI: Strengthening Institutional Capability for Climate Finance in the Pacific (Pacific)
descriptions: A major barrier to access, absorb and deliver climate finance is limited institutional preparedness and capability in key institutions such as government ministries, national funds, regional and national accredited entities, and development banks. This means that even when climate finance is approved there can be considerable delays in deploying this funding. New mandates for fast-tracking climate finance delivery and implementation stemming from COP26 signalled that increased finance flows are about to be available to Small Island Developing States (SIDS). The next five years is therefore critical for unlocking access to finance in Pacific Island Countries (PICs) and supporting them to strengthen absorption and delivery capacity to enable implementation before 2030. This project, The Global Green Growth Initiative, aims to enhance the capacity and institutional capability of PICS and institutions to access climate finance and increased absorptive capacity for efficient delivery of impactful climate programmes.

titles: Oxygen CoLab Phase 2: Implementation Phase and Overall Lessons Learning from Co-Labs Approach in ODA-Eligible Countries
Oxygen CoLab Phase 2: Implementation Phase and overall lessons learning from Co-labs approach
descriptions: This work goes beyond the COVID-19 response to the long-term strengthening of systems and preparedness for future pandemics. Phase 1 of the Oxygen CoLab will advance the research and development of oxygen concentrators for low-resource settings, whilst also ensuring the business model (Oxygen as a Service) and financial sustainability of those products is being tested and validated. The goal is to contribute to accelerated and sustained access to fit for purpose oxygen concentrators in underserved health centres and hospitals. It will work concurrently across three key workstreams: 1) Accelerate product innovation: Creating an accelerated path to market for fit for purpose oxygen concentrator innovations. 2) Catalyse market traction: Putting oxygen concentrators on the path to sustainable scale in our focus countries, through coaching and funding grantee innovators; evidence-based in-country advocacy; and generating interest and confidence from both country and global stakeholders in innovative financing and alternative business models. 3) Enable a collective response and anticipatory action: Supporting a local and global conversation about oxygen provision, and contributing to a movement for fit for purpose oxygen concentrators.

titles: Building Stability Planning Component
descriptions: Justice and Stability in the Sahel (JASS) programme phase 1 (Sept. 2021 – March 2023) overall objective is improving security and stability in the Sahel. The programme aimed to prevent the spread of violent conflict in the Sahel by addressing underlying factors such as perception of marginalisation by certain population groups, lack of legitimacy of governance mechanisms on resource allocation and access, and the increased demographic competition for natural resources without sufficient economic diversification. The JASS programme intervened in 12 communes in the central regions of Segou, Koulikoro and Sikasso in Mali towards three contributory outcomes: 1) improved conflict management capacity and collaboration amongst communities, as well as between communities and institutions; 2) addressing climate-related pressures on land and natural resources that are driving factors for increased conflict across the Sahel; 3)  conducting research that help to underpin the JASS evidence base and confirmed that assumptions underlying the programme's theory of change hold true.

The programme will build upon existing UK support to conflict resolution funded via the Conflict Stability and Security Fund (CSSF) in Mali and will take a phased approach. Phase I will respond to the most pressing and central to conflict dynamics, but also make preparations (identify the partners, develop the evidence base and test approaches) for a larger more ambitious programme to begin in 12-18 months.

titles: Justice and Stability in the Sahel (JASS) Phase 2

titles: Sharing lessons learned from Brazil’s Social Protection response to COVID-19
descriptions: A one-year programme funding the World Bank to analyse, document and disseminate Brazil’s successful experience with the emergency benefit to protect vulnerable populations from the economic impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic.  Although Brazil has had difficulties controlling the spread of the virus, its emergency cash transfer programme (Auxilio Emergencial, AE) has been one of the largest and most rapidly deployed social protection programmes in the world, helping 67 million informal workers who would otherwise have struggled badly. titles: National Governance Programme.  Implementation through technical assistance
descriptions: The proposed intervention will work at the core of government, reinforcing critical governance mechanisms at federal level. It will strengthen the institutions mandated to coordinate between the federal and provincial levels of government, allocate and distribute resources between them in an equitable manner, and will improve coordination between ministries including for anticipating and responding to crises. It will also explore supporting the Parliament exercise its oversight better. The proposed intervention is mostly geared towards addressing “how” the institutions of governance work rather than “what” they are working on. The intervention is non-sectoral, but it is expected to have visible results in critical areas such as the ability of the government to continue to successfully steer the country through the ongoing crises, and in sectors relevant to UK’s priorities in Pakistan, such as population dynamics, the economy and work on climate adaptation and resilience.

This project is being jointly funded by the Dutch Ministry of Foreign Affairs (BZ).

titles: (CVIM) Accelerating development of novel vaccines via support to the UK Centre for Veterinary Vaccine Innovation & Manufacturing
descriptions:
The Centre for Veterinary Vaccine Innovation & Manufacturing (CVIM) has been set up to bridge a gap between basic research and late-stage product development of vaccines. New technology (for example RNA vaccines) has the potential to transform vaccine development, but currently low-cost livestock vaccines utilising emerging technology are not being developed for deployment in developing countries. The overall objective of the centre is to accelerate the development and production of vaccines for the most challenging, and urgent livestock diseases, including those that can spread to humans (zoonotic diseases) and cause significant productivity loss in Low- and Middle-income Countries (LMICs). 
By accelerating the development of novel vaccines for high consequence livestock diseases with commercial partners in both developed and developing countries, the programme will improve vaccine access and use and consequently improve the livelihoods of livestock farmers and economic wellbeing and food security in LIDCs. It will enable international trade and protect human health. 
The programme will build on existing capability at the Pirbright Institute, UK, leveraging Pirbright’s high containment facilities for laboratory and animal studies and expertise in veterinary virology, immunology, and vaccine development.

The Centre for Veterinary Vaccine Innovation & Manufacturing (CVIM), a specialized veterinary manufacturing research and development facility, will have the following overall objectives: A) To establish a vital element of the UK's pandemic preparedness programme by emergency response vaccine development and production capacity for orphan livestock and zoonotic diseases of high consequence, newly emerging zoonotic viral diseases and limiting their spread and impact on livestock and humans B) Address niche markets in developing countries where there is an important clinical need for new vaccines but where it is commercially challenging C) Bridge the gaps between research and downstream commercial development of vaccines by supporting manufacturing innovation to reduce costs, scale production, and support adoption of novel platform technologies, thereby accelerating the development of animal and human vaccines D) Establish the utility of novel vaccine platform technologies for neglected livestock diseases and urgent emerging zoonotic diseases, that currently have insufficient commercial drive to justify industry investment E) To develop CVIM’s reputation as a leading international pilot-scale manufacturing Centre, able to attract, train and retain world class scientific, manufacturing, and regulatory expertise, and share this expertise nationally and internationally
